{"id": "22:40/q49", "question": "When and why was permission to fight first given?", "turns_on": "The occasion reports and placement arguments relate expulsion to a new permission for defensive fighting.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q49/p1", "position": "After the Prophet's departure and Quraysh's persecution, 22:39–40 first permitted fighting.", "reasons": "Urwa and others say Muslims had been ordered to call, endure, and pardon. Ibn Abbas reports Abu Bakr's fear and recognition that fighting would follow. Ibn Zayd says the reprieve lasted ten years."}, {"id": "22:40/q49/p2", "position": "It permitted fighting those who blocked the emigrants' migration.", "reasons": "Mujahid relates this to specific Meccan emigrants."}, {"id": "22:40/q49/p3", "position": "It permitted defense if Quraysh barred pilgrimage to the House, including fighting in the Haram or sacred months.", "reasons": "Islahi says Quraysh used sanctuary rules as a shield while occupying Abraham's House and accusing Muslims of impiety."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q50", "question": "Was this verse revealed in Mecca or Medina?", "turns_on": "Destination of exile and the disputed dating of the sūra.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q50/p1", "position": "This passage was revealed in Medina, after migration.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur is certain; Islahi says 22:38–41 are Medinan explanatory verses within a Makkan sura."}, {"id": "22:40/q50/p2", "position": "The expulsion to Abyssinia would make the verse Meccan.", "reasons": "Tabrisi records this alternative."}, {"id": "22:40/q50/p3", "position": "The sura as a whole is Madinan except 52–55.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports one dating view."}, {"id": "22:40/q50/p4", "position": "The sura is Makkan except 19–22.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports another dating view."}, {"id": "22:40/q50/p5", "position": "The sura mixes Makkan and Madinan verses.", "reasons": "Study Quran says most authorities hold this; a tradition describes revelation by day and night, travel and home, war and peace."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q51", "question": "How does this clause connect with its context?", "turns_on": "Its relation to 22:39 and 22:41 and the wider argument about the House.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q51/p1", "position": "It parallels God's checking people in 2:251 and other statements of religious defense.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan invokes David and Goliath; Elmalili links otherwise-destroyed sanctuaries to corruption of earth. Notes referring back to 2:251 preserve the link. Samin directs readers to 2:251 on the parallel readings."}, {"id": "22:40/q51/p2", "position": "It explains and honors the new permission to fight after persecution and expulsion.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur calls the waw parenthetical and resumptive, and Biqa'i attaches the later promise either here or to the permission in 22:39. Kashshaf and Uthman call the following praise of empowered emigrants advance praise; Uthman applies it to his companions."}, {"id": "22:40/q51/p3", "position": "It answers Quraysh's claim to Abraham's House and their charge that fighting there is impious.", "reasons": "Islahi says Abraham founded the House for monotheistic worship, Quraysh distorted it, and these Medinan verses answer the threat that they would obstruct pilgrimage."}, {"id": "22:40/q51/p4", "position": "The following account of earlier messengers consoles Muhammad after the account of expulsion.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls this a second consolation."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q52", "question": "What unusual reports accompany the permission and later praise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q52/p1", "position": "Uthman said the verse and its sequel describe him and companions later empowered for prayer, alms, and right action.", "reasons": "The report calls the praise advance praise before the deeds."}, {"id": "22:40/q52/p2", "position": "At the trench, Muslims and the Prophet chanted a plea for guidance and firmness.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports the Prophet repeating the line's ending during digging."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q01", "question": "Which communities are meant by 'every community'?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression ranges over successive nations or contemporary religious groups.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q01/p1", "position": "Successive communities, past through the Prophet's community, each under its own messenger or law.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī calls them past generations; Bursevī includes past and future nations sent messengers. Rāzī allows all nations whether traces survive; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says succession rather than simultaneous distinct laws because Muhammad's mission is universal."}, {"id": "22:67/q01/p2", "position": "Religious communities, including people of other religions living with Muhammad.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī defines an umma by religion; Rāzī reports the narrower view that only Jews and Christians with extant revealed law are meant."}, {"id": "22:67/q01/p3", "position": "An umma is a group of forty to one hundred or more.", "reasons": "Abū al-Malīḥ supplies the numerical gloss."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q02", "question": "What is the appointed mansak?", "turns_on": "Whether mansak denotes law or action, sacrifice, festival, or a ritual place or time; context and 'they perform it' are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q02/p1", "position": "A distinct religious law or path prescribed for each community.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for law; Rāzī prefers it via ʿAṭāʾ and al-Qaffāl, citing 5:48, the breadth of worship, all pilgrimage rites, and 'they practice it'. Alūsī and Bursevī infer exclusivity from fronting 'for every community'; Kuran Yolu adopts the broad sense because context does not require restriction. Islahi includes worship forms and principles; Asad points to 5:48."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p2", "position": "A sacrifice or the shedding of sacrificial blood.", "reasons": "Muqātil describes festival bloodshed and cites 6:162 for nusuk. Mujāhid specifies blood in Mecca. Ṭabarī prefers offerings at Mina on Nahr days because the pagans disputed that rite; ordinary slaughter in al-Anʿām is no rite. Al-Ḥākim grades ʿAlī ibn al-Ḥusayn's slaughter report sound. Kuran Yolu observes verse 34 encourages this reading."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p3", "position": "A prescribed rite comprising pilgrimage and sacrifice.", "reasons": "Qatāda gives both Hajj and slaughter; Ṭabarī refers also to 22:34."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p4", "position": "A festival or feast day, sometimes one with an animal sacrifice.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Qutayba are cited; Rāzī specifies a festival at which slaughter occurs. Kuran Yolu relays Ṭabarī's festival report."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p5", "position": "A customary place of worship or ritual, especially sacrifice or pilgrimage sites.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī derives it from a place habitually frequented for good or evil, and Hajj sites from repeated visits; Thaʿlabī, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr and Biqāʿī repeat this. Al-Farrāʾ specifies Hajj and ʿumra sites; al-Ḍaḥḥāk a slaughter place; Ṭabrisī includes Mina or elsewhere. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes it as pilgrimage sites here but sacrifice site at 22:34, opposing idol-specific shrines; Kuran Yolu agrees."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p6", "position": "Worship or a ritual act, encompassing acts of devotion.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan equates nusuk with worship and nāsik with worshipper; Jishumī distinguishes nusuk, nāsik and nasīka. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ṭabāṭabāʾī invoke 'they perform it' for a verbal noun; Asad and Study Quran allow an act of worship."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p7", "position": "An appointed time for worship.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports the time alternative alongside place; Alūsī records it among lexical proposals."}, {"id": "22:67/q02/p8", "position": "Ironically, an obstinate nation's customary path, even a wrongful one.", "reasons": "Alūsī reports this as consolation to the Prophet; Biqāʿī says a community may gather around its desires against God's command."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q03", "question": "How is mansak read and justified?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun follows the regular verbal or place noun pattern or an attested exceptional/dialect form.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q03/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on the sīn: mansak.", "reasons": "The other readers use it at both occurrences. Al-Fārisī prefers it because verbal and place nouns of this pattern normally take fatḥa; Ibn Khālawayh gives the same pattern argument. Ṭabarī calls it the Asad dialect. Jishumī calls it a verbal noun for shedding sacrificial blood; Ibn ʿĀshūr a place noun with both mīm and sīn open."}, {"id": "22:67/q03/p2", "position": "With kasra on the sīn: mansik.", "reasons": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read it thus at both occurrences; al-Nashr adds Khalaf. Ṭabarī calls it a Hijaz form; Ibn Khālawayh derives it from a slaughter site. Al-Fārisī allows an exceptional mafʿil place noun like maṭliʿ or masjid if attested and suggests al-Kisāʾī heard it; Qiraat ER calls it a canonical place or time noun."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q04", "question": "How does 'they perform it' attach to mansak?", "turns_on": "Whether a direct object pronoun excludes a place noun or a locative may be governed directly.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q04/p1", "position": "It is an adjective clause for mansak and its direct object favors an act or verbal noun.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī argue a place would require 'worshippers in it'; Rāzī likewise says the construction fits worship rather than a specific place or time. Samīn identifies the adjective clause; Ṭabāṭabāʾī uses the phrase for the worship sense."}, {"id": "22:67/q04/p2", "position": "It can describe a place: the locative is made a direct object by extension or omission of 'in'.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya's necessity: active participles can govern locatives directly, illustrated by an anonymous poem's mashrab and travel over two farsakhs. Samīn cites poems with 'a day we witnessed' and 'a drinking place I drink'; Ibn ʿĀshūr analyzes omission of the preposition."}]}

": "22:67/q05", "question": "What does the clause say about those performing the rite?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q05/p1", "position": "Each designated community follows or performs its own assigned law or rite.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Alūsī take the pronoun and adjective clause to reinforce exclusive allocation, comparing separate garments; their sequence is Torah until Jesus, Gospel until Muhammad, then Qurʾān until Judgment. Nasafī simply says they perform the sacrifice; Bayḍāwī says they perform the worship."}, {"id": "22:67/q05/p2", "position": "Their performance occurs by God's decree and should not trouble the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr compares the diversity to 2:148 and says God's will governs their rites."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q06", "question": "What does the verse teach about changing religious laws?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse's shared object is the full law of successive communities or specifically a recurring sacrificial rite.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q06/p1", "position": "God assigns different laws to successive communities; earlier laws yield to Muhammad's universal law.", "reasons": "Rāzī says living adherents must follow Muhammad. Qurṭubī cites differences across eras. Bursevī and Alūsī detail the Torah–Gospel–Qurʾān sequence. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says successors' greater readiness brought better rites. Islahi says change reforms invented practices and tests sincerity; Kuran Yolu says rulings suit circumstances and development. Ibn Kathīr also states that God appointed a rite for every community."}, {"id": "22:67/q06/p2", "position": "God prescribed sacrifice for every community, establishing it as a genuine ancient rite.", "reasons": "Nasafī uses this to refute those denying sacrifice is part of divine law; Alūsī reports that its antiquity answers pagan objection. Shaykh al-Islām objects that restricting the dispute to sacrifices would falsely treat carrion and pagan practices as divinely assigned rites."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q07", "question": "Who are the disputants?", "turns_on": "The reported occasion points to pagans and slaughter, while the law interpretation points to scriptural communities.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q07/p1", "position": "Polytheists, including Quraysh or Khuzāʿa, challenge Muhammad and the Muslims.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Khuzāʿa and others; Ibn al-Jawzī names Quraysh and Khuzāʿa. Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers polytheists from the continuing pronouns to 22:72 and the mixed dating; he finds People of the Book less likely. Several reports supply named leaders."}, {"id": "22:67/q07/p2", "position": "People of earlier revealed scriptures argue from inherited Torah or Gospel.", "reasons": "Bursevī and Alūsī say their laws have been abrogated; Islahi says Jews and Christians sided with Quraysh and fueled debate."}, {"id": "22:67/q07/p3", "position": "Adherents of other religions generally dispute with the Prophet.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī describes them as ignorant or obstinate; Tabatabaʾī describes unbelievers denying the Prophet's authority."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q08", "question": "What is the 'matter' under dispute?", "turns_on": "The topic varies with whether mansak is read as sacrifice, law, or pilgrimage place.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q08/p1", "position": "Slaughter, sacrificial animals, and whether carrion may be eaten.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī and Mujāhid connect it to sacrifice and the pagans' meat argument; Qatāda says not to avoid one's slaughtered meat. Ibn ʿAṭiyya makes this follow the sacrifice-site reading. Alūsī reports a view grounding the response in sacrifice's antiquity."}, {"id": "22:67/q08/p2", "position": "Religion, the Prophet's message, or rites and law generally.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya makes religion or scripture follow the law reading. Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān allow religion; Bayḍāwī includes religious rites. Bursevī and Alūsī identify the inherited laws and their abrogation. Biqāʿī includes satanic objections to abrogation."}, {"id": "22:67/q08/p3", "position": "Monotheism, including whether pagan pilgrimage proves pagan religion true.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr infers monotheism from the surrounding evidence and distinguishes valid pilgrimage from later idol rites."}, {"id": "22:67/q08/p4", "position": "The proper pilgrimage standing place: Quraysh at Muzdalifah versus others at Arafat.", "reasons": "Mālik identifies the contest; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites a Muwaṭṭaʾ occasion report."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q09", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported?", "turns_on": "The reports identify different concrete disputes, meat or pilgrimage standing.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q09/p1", "position": "Khuzāʿī or Quraysh leaders asked why Muslims eat animals they slaughter but reject carrion, which they said God killed.", "reasons": "Muqātil names Badīl ibn Warqāʾ, Bishr ibn Sufyān, and Yazīd ibn al-Ḥalbas of Banū al-Ḥārith; Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, and Baghawī give Yazīd ibn al-Khunays/Khunays; Jishumī gives Yazīd ibn Waraqah. Some accounts name only Khuzāʿa or polytheists. The names vary; the challenge is shared."}, {"id": "22:67/q09/p2", "position": "A pilgrimage dispute between Quraysh at Qazah in Muzdalifah and other Arabs at Arafat occasioned it.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr quotes the Muwaṭṭaʾ from people of knowledge; Mālik connects the standing-place dispute to this verse. Ibn al-Zubayr defines valid standing areas, except ʿUrana and Muḥassir valleys."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q10", "question": "When was the injunction or its occasion?", "turns_on": "The dating depends on the inferred relation to fighting or the pilgrimage occasion.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q10/p1", "position": "The instruction preceded fighting.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj infers this from the following instruction about what to say if they argue; Wāḥidī relays him."}, {"id": "22:67/q10/p2", "position": "On the pilgrimage-occasion account, it came after Hajj became obligatory and before polytheists were barred, in year nine.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Bājī following Rabīʿa, but says the stronger dating differs without specifying it in this note."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q11", "question": "What does the verb of disputation mean lexically?", "turns_on": "Whether ordinary mutual disputation or a special 'prevail in dispute' derivation is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q11/p1", "position": "Mutual contention or argument.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the direct gloss; Bursevī derives contention from pulling something from its place. Al-Zajjāj illustrates opposing and prevailing in nāzaʿanī fa-nazaʿtuhu and ʿāzzanī fa-ʿazaztuhu."}, {"id": "22:67/q11/p2", "position": "Contending until one party prevails over the other.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's derivation is reported by Samīn and Alūsī. Alūsī notes grammarians reject a claimed guttural exception in the verb pattern and cites Sībawayh that the prevailing pattern is not universal."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q12", "question": "How is 'let them not dispute with you' to be understood?", "turns_on": "The reciprocal verb can aim at opponents, indirectly restrain the Prophet, or urge firmness; syntax and the next verse are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q12/p1", "position": "A real prohibition to the opponents: they must not contest Muhammad's prescribed religion or rites.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī reasons laws differ by era. Alūsī prefers the apparent address to opponents; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the opening supplies its argument despite unbelievers denying his authority. Bayḍāwī says opponents are ignorant or obstinate."}, {"id": "22:67/q12/p2", "position": "An indirect command to the Prophet to avoid engaging in mutual argument.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites the following 'if they argue' and says a reciprocal verb can forbid either participant, unlike 'strike'; Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr repeat it. Ibn ʿAṭiyya relates a threat reading but prefers belittling the disputants; Qurṭubī compares not fighting back."}, {"id": "22:67/q12/p3", "position": "Do not heed or be drawn into their contentious debate; continue steadfast in religion.", "reasons": "Yahyā says polytheists must not turn him away; Ibn Jinnī says the common wording orders certainty and ignoring false claims. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers belittling those too insignificant for debate; Bayḍāwī says debate suits truth seekers, not obstinate people. Ibn Kathīr says their disputes must neither trouble nor divert him."}, {"id": "22:67/q12/p4", "position": "A rhetorical prohibition aimed at opponents through the Prophet: give them no occasion to dispute.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes the idiom 'do not let me find you doing this'; Abū Ḥayyān compares 'do not let me see you here'; Ibn ʿAṭiyya gives the implied statement that they lack power to dispute."}, {"id": "22:67/q12/p5", "position": "Keep debating resolutely so opponents do not defeat you in argument.", "reasons": "Alūsī draws this force from al-Zajjāj's proposed 'prevail' derivation, while reporting the grammatical objection to that derivation."}]}
{"id": "22:67/q13", "question": "What variant readings occur in the prohibition?", "turns_on": "The readings differ in the verb root, mutual contention versus pulling away, and reported nūn weight.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q13/p1", "position": "The common reading is fa-lā yunāziʿannaka, with a light nūn also reported.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī glosses the common reading as standing firm and ignoring falsehood, citing the 'do not let me see you' idiom and al-Nābigha. Samīn and Alūsī report light nūn; Abū Ḥayyān says this reading tells the Prophet to resist enticement."}, {"id": "22:67/q13/p2", "position": "Abū Majliz reads fa-lā yanziʿannaka, 'let them not pull you away' from your religion.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj also records the form; Ibn Jinnī relates it to selection by belief and knowledge, with 30:60 and 19:69, rather than physical pulling. Alūsī adds Lāḥiq ibn Ḥumayd and kasra on zāy; Qurṭubī describes being snatched or overpowered."}]}

{"id": "22:67/q18", "question": "How does 22:67 connect with the earlier 'for every community' at 22:34 and the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Explanations differ on whether the opening resumes rites, marks distance, or belongs to the sūra's disputation theme.", "positions": [{"id": "22:67/q18/p1", "position": "It resumes the earlier discussion of prescribed rites and sacrifice, with intervening material separating the statements.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 22:34, 22:37–38 and says the relation is clear enough to omit a conjunction. Al-Kashf links prior pilgrims' benefits and remembrance in 22:28; al-Ṭībī links honoring rites in 22:32. Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī refer back to 22:34. Rāzī says the passage turns from mercy despite ingratitude to the favor of prescribed duties."}, {"id": "22:67/q18/p2", "position": "The absent conjunction marks semantic distance from the earlier sacrificial context.", "reasons": "Rāzī says this independent sentence is not attached to what precedes. Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts 22:34, which had a conjunction because nearby verses related to sacrifice, with this more distant context; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn relay it."}, {"id": "22:67/q18/p3", "position": "The connection is complete because prior evidence establishes that disputing God's ruling is unbelief.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī cites 2:106 and reads the opening without conjunction accordingly."}, {"id": "22:67/q18/p4", "position": "The verse belongs to a wider consolation and disputation sequence.", "reasons": "Alūsī reports a link back to unbelievers' doubt in 22:55 and divine judgment in 22:69; al-Kashf objects that 22:60 does not reinforce consolation; Alūsī rejects that link as far-fetched and instead points to the sūra's recurring argument with obstinate opponents beginning at 22:3. The sūra's close exposes shirk and urges worship and striving."}]}

{"id": "23:13/q01", "question": "What does thumma mark in this creation sequence?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is explained by the stage's rank and marvel or by the interval between stages.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q01/p1", "position": "It marks the remarkable transition from clay to reproductive fluid or the higher rank of placing that fluid in the womb.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī calls water humanity's second, purer origin and the source of life, and calls the transition striking. {"id": "23:13/q02", "question": "How does jaʿalnāhu function grammatically and semantically here?", "turns_on": "The sense assigned to jaʿala and the syntactic role of nuṭfa and the prepositional phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q02/p1", "position": "Jaʿala means 'make' with nuṭfa as its second object.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls this the majority analysis. Biqāʿī says jaʿala conveys producing a result through a cause."}, {"id": "23:13/q02/p2", "position": "Jaʿala means 'place'; nuṭfa is circumstantial and the phrase 'in a firm lodging' is its second object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr argues that fī expresses placement of reproductive material in the womb, hence jaʿala rather than khalq; nuṭfa is accusative as a circumstantial expression."}, {"id": "23:13/q02/p3", "position": "Jaʿala means 'create,' and nuṭfa is accusative after an omitted preposition.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that some investigators favor this analysis."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q03", "question": "Who or what does the pronoun in jaʿalnāhu refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the antecedent is Adam with an understood descendant, the inclusive human kind, or the preceding extracted substance; Ālūsī weighs the need for an omitted antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q03/p1", "position": "It refers to Adam's offspring or a descendant, supplied by context even though Adam or 'human' was named previously.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Zajjāj, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, Qurṭubī, Burhān, and Itqān say Adam himself was not a drop. Wāḥidī's Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm licenses the shift by context; Wāḥidī compares 5:101. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Qurṭubī compare 38:32. Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Bursevī, Samīn, and Ālūsī report supplying an omitted 'offspring' or possessive; Nasafī cites 32:7–8. Qatāda's clay Adam and fluid descendants are reported by Durr. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the shift from Adam to his descendants an ancestral reference. Ālūsī finds an unstated son of Adam or omitted possessive strained; Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects limiting 'human' to descendants, arguing that this would call for 'created him as a drop.'"}, {"id": "23:13/q03/p2", "position": "It refers to humankind as a species, with Adam's origin and the descendants' reproductive origin treated together.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, as reported by Samīn, lets each pronoun select the relevant origin or descendants. Ibn Kathīr cites 32:7–8; Bursevī speaks of individuals distinct from Adam. Ālūsī prefers this because it avoids strained omitted antecedents. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid reading al-insān generically. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers the inclusive kind and cites 32:7–8, rejecting restriction to Adam alone or descendants alone. Elmalılı allows humankind or its progeny."}, {"id": "23:13/q03/p3", "position": "It refers to the extracted clay substance, made into a drop.", "reasons": "Zajjāj reports Adam's semen as the clay-derived extract; Bayḍāwī interprets the masculine pronoun as a substance, extracted thing, or water. Biqāʿī allows the clay itself; Ālūsī and Elmalılı report the extract reading."}, {"id": "23:13/q03/p4", "position": "It refers to the human formed from the extract, whose reproductive substance God places in the womb.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the pronoun from the human derived from the preceding extract and reads the clause as placement in a lodging."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q04", "question": "What does nuṭfa mean in Arabic and in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether nuṭfa is read by its general water sense, male seminal fluid, the particular seed or zygote, or combined reproductive material.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q04/p1", "position": "It is the small drop of reproductive fluid, commonly a man's semen.", "reasons": "Māwardī specifies male fluid from which a child forms by adhering. Jishumī derives the root from dripping and cites nuṭūf for a rainy night. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Jishumī, Nasafī, Study Quran, and Ibn Kathīr identify seminal or weak fluid; Ibn Kathīr cites 77:20, and Study Quran lists 16:4, 18:37, 22:5, 35:11, 36:77, 40:67, 53:46, 75:37, 76:2, 80:19. Biqāʿī notes the flowing drop has no visible clay."}, {"id": "23:13/q04/p2", "position": "It can mean water generally, little or much, or clear pure water.", "reasons": "Māwardī cites a Hudhayl poet's thirsty drinkers for ordinary water. Jishumī mentions an account of a rider between the eastern and western seas as evidence of wide water usage. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says little or great quantity; Bursevī calls it clear, pure water; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says a little water and sometimes water generally."}, {"id": "23:13/q04/p3", "position": "In this verse it specifically denotes the seed within semen or the fertilized zygote.", "reasons": "Elmalılı argues that what actually settles in the womb is the seed, not semen as a whole. Kur'an Yolu describes sperm fertilizing the ovum, with the resultant zygote called nuṭfa as it reaches the womb."}, {"id": "23:13/q04/p4", "position": "The drop stage involves the union of male and female reproductive extracts.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr traces the extracts through earth-derived nourishment, blood, male semen and female ova; he says the male fluid is named for dripping through its channel into the womb. Ibn Kathīr reports a Prophetic answer that male thick fluid makes bones and sinews while female thin fluid makes flesh and blood, confirmed by a Jewish questioner."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q05", "question": "How is fī qarārin makīn attached syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether the prepositional phrase completes the verb or qualifies the drop.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q05/p1", "position": "The phrase attaches to jaʿalnāhu.", "reasons": "Samīn gives this as one permissible attachment; Ibn ʿĀshūr analyzes it as the second object when jaʿala means place."}, {"id": "23:13/q05/p2", "position": "It is an omitted adjective of nuṭfa.", "reasons": "Samīn gives this as the alternative grammatical attachment."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q06", "question": "What does qarār mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q06/p1", "position": "It is a place of settling or residence, expressed by a verbal noun used as a place name.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Rāzī, Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī note the verbal noun; Bursevī, Ālūsī, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī see emphatic force. {"id": "23:13/q07", "question": "What is the qarār makīn, the drop's secure lodging?", "turns_on": "Whether the lodging names only the womb or includes earlier sites through which the generative material passes.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q07/p1", "position": "It is the womb, prepared to receive, retain, and protect the embryo until its appointed term.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Thaʿlabī, Māwardī, Wāḥidī citing Ibn ʿAbbās and commentators, Wāḥidī's Wajīz, Jishumī, Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn, Ibn Kathīr, Bursevī, Ālūsī, Elmalılı, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Kur'an Yolu, and Study Quran identify the womb. Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Baghawī, Ibn Kathīr and Jishumī stress its preparation and fixed term; Ibn Kathīr cites 77:21–23. Ibn al-Jawzī points to explanations of the stages at 22:5."}, {"id": "23:13/q07/p2", "position": "The secure receptacle includes the fathers' loins and ribs before the womb.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī extends the lodging across the route of reproductive fluid, emphasizing protection from corrupting influences."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q08", "question": "What does makīn describe and why is the lodging secure?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective names the womb's own stability or transfers the secure position of what it contains.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q08/p1", "position": "It describes the womb's own fixed, fortified, protective position and ability to retain its contents.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī reports al-Mufaḍḍal's 'firmly settled, not unstable.' Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it is firmly situated."}, {"id": "23:13/q08/p2", "position": "It transfers the security or settledness of the drop or occupant to its lodging.", "reasons": "Rāzī allows transfer from what settles there; Bayḍāwī says the term is applied emphatically to the location; Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn compare calling a road 'travelling'; Bursevī describes the womb by its contents' quality; Ālūsī calls the attribution to the drop metaphorical; Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows the drop's secure position."}]}

{"id": "23:13/q11", "question": "What does the creation sequence show about human development?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize different aspects of one sequence: bodily differentiation, transmission from earth through reproductive material, or the change from first creation to reproduction.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q11/p1", "position": "A uniform drop is differentiated into a complex body through successive measured stages.", "reasons": "Qushayrī lists flesh, bone, hair, nails, nerves, skin, brain, and veins with each member's form. Rāzī counts nine stages. Elmalılı distinguishes the first extraordinary origin from subsequent customary natural formation. Kur'an Yolu describes soil-derived food and plants through gestation, with sperm, ovum, and zygote; İslāḥī says science has uncovered aspects only hinted at, and Sāmarrāʾī says embryonic descriptions accord with modern anatomy and medicine. Biqāʿī reports al-Ḥarālī's account of measured components appearing as a form after mixture and applies it to clay."}, {"id": "23:13/q11/p2", "position": "The clay origin passes through fathers' semen into the mother's womb.", "reasons": "Rāzī describes clay becoming semen in fathers' loins and being conveyed by intercourse. Nasafī reports another view in which 'human' means Adam's children, sulāla means semen extracted ultimately from clay through Adam; Ibn ʿĀshūr traces earth-derived nourishment into the combined reproductive extracts."}, {"id": "23:13/q11/p3", "position": "Creation changes mode from the first clay-formed human to reproduction through a lowly drop.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes the change of mode; Elmalılı cites 32:8 for the first human followed by offspring from fluid. Wāḥidī's Wajīz calls the drop the start of an individual's formation. Elmalılı elsewhere calls fluid the nearest and clearest starting point for reflection, though technically the second stage."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q12", "question": "Does the creation account support a claim about what a human being is?", "turns_on": "These are distinct claims about bodily identity and the later emergence of human capacities.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q12/p1", "position": "Its description of bodily formation opposes theories that a human is only spirit or a nonbodily indivisible entity.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī names al-Naẓẓām's spirit view and Maʿmar's indivisible nonbodily view as contradicted by the passage."}, {"id": "23:13/q12/p2", "position": "The later human is transformed from lifeless, ignorant, powerless matter into a living, knowing, capable being.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the pronoun in the following 'We brought him into being' refers to the human whose bones were clothed with flesh."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q13", "question": "What does the sequence teach about the cause of natural development?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q13/p1", "position": "God's creative power governs nature and causes its changes, including development from clay and drop.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says nature is internal to a thing and cannot externally cause its own transformation; stable natures require an outside influence to change. {"id": "23:13/q14", "question": "How does this account argue for resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q14/p1", "position": "The God who formed people through these stages can recreate them after death; the ordered process displays power and wisdom.", "reasons": "İslāḥī says deniers mock afterlife promises, yet creation from a drop and familiar development into learned people such as Socrates, Hippocrates, Aristotle, and Galen cannot plausibly be accidental or meaningless. He cites 22:5 and its 'so that We make evident for you,' invites reflection on one's own body, and says this passage elaborates the same proof. Rāzī treats development as one of several proofs. Biqāʿī describes the sūra's turn from Paradise to first creation, cosmos, earlier peoples, gratitude, resurrection, and oneness. Study Quran's introduction recalls the stages and 22:5."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q15", "question": "How does the creation passage fit the sūra's argument and adjacent verses?", "turns_on": "The notes link the account either to the sūra's ongoing exhortation or to parallel origin and resurrection passages.", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q15/p1", "position": "After believers and their promised reward, creation and provision show God's sole lordship and invite gratitude and worship.", "reasons": "Jishumī connects prior afterlife blessings to blessings at human origins. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the passage opens a new proof against polytheists after 23:1, contrasting grateful believers with ungrateful idolaters. Ṭabāṭabāʾī similarly says God alone deserves worship. Kur'an Yolu calls for gratitude; İslāḥī notes the earlier glad tidings and their rejection. Biqāʿī traces the sūra's larger movement through creation, cosmos, earlier peoples, and resurrection; Noah begins the narrative because he was the first prophet and the ark rescue recalls humanity's descent from him, while the next sūra continues the theme of guarding sexual integrity. Study Quran notes the recurrent opposition of powerful and affluent people to prophets."}, {"id": "23:13/q15/p2", "position": "The passage recalls other Qur'anic descriptions of origin from earth and a drop, especially 22:5 and 32:7–8.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 18:37 and 22:5. Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, Elmalılı, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī cite 32:7–8 or 32:8 for clay then offspring from fluid. Qurṭubī and Ibn al-Jawzī refer discussion of the drop, clot, morsel, and legal rulings back to commentary on Sūrat al-Ḥajj. İslāḥī says the present passage develops the argument of 22:5 further."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q16", "question": "Why are the creation verbs expressed as past events?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q16/p1", "position": "The past form can emphasize that the statement is certain, while the process continues in each person.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu renders the Arabic past verbs in the present to convey ongoing creation and says Qur'anic past forms can mark certainty."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q17", "question": "Why is creation more emphatically stated than resurrection in this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q17/p1", "position": "Creation is foregrounded and death recurs more often, so creation receives two emphases and resurrection one; resurrection is easier than first origination, though both are easy for God.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī makes the comparison with 39:30 and ties the distribution of emphasis to this sūra's context."}]}
{"id": "23:13/q18", "question": "Why does the passage state what the polytheists already know?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:13/q18/p1", "position": "Its emphatic opening addresses them as though they denied creation, because they fail to act on that knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr points to the oath lām and emphatic particle in the passage's opening."}]}

{"id": "23:14/q02", "question": "What is the nutfa and how does it become the next stage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q02/p1", "position": "The reproductive fluid develops in the womb into the red clot.", "reasons": "Muqātil describes fluid becoming blood; al-Ṭabarī says the secure womb holds it to its appointed development (23:13); al-Rāzī treats the change as new qualities and accidents; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, Bursevī describe white semen turning red. {"id": "23:14/q03", "question": "What does ʿalaqa mean and why is it called that?", "turns_on": "Whether the term describes blood, attachment, leech-like appearance, or their combination.", "positions": [{"id": "23:14/q03/p1", "position": "A piece of blood, congealed or clotted, that becomes the embryo.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba calls it one clot, singular of ʿalaq; al-Māwardī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya call it fresh blood; Jishumī distinguishes congealed from flowing blood.
